metadata.title: Exploring the optimal factors influencing teachers’ instructional practices performance using machine learning approaches

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 microdata for secondary school teachers in Shanghai, China, with a sample of 3,976 teachers across 198 schools in 16 districts. The manuscript describes exporting data in Stata and recoding the dependent variable, but it does not report applying TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme. Because the analysis is based on machine-learning classifiers (Random Forest, GBM, XGBoost) and the paper does not specify weight-aware estimation, it is unclear whether complex survey design weights were used; analysts should consult the TALIS 2018 Data User Guide for the appropriate teacher weight variable(s) and replicate weights if variance estimation is required. The preprocessing explicitly includes mode imputation for missing values and feature selection via RFECV and domain-knowledge refinement, which should be performed within the training folds to avoid leakage (the paper does not fully specify fold-level imputation/feature-selection ordering).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a binary classification derived from TALIS instructional-practices indicator scores (above-mean vs below-mean), not a PV-based cognitive achievement scale. Missing-data handling is reported as mode imputation, which is a form of single-value imputation for categorical variables; however, the paper does not report the proportion of missingness or whether imputation was conducted within cross-validation folds, which limits assessment of potential bias or leakage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher data for Shanghai, China, restricted to secondary school teachers (3,976 teachers across 198 schools in 16 districts). The dependent variable (T3TPRA/“Teaching Practices”) was recoded into a binary outcome: teachers with instructional-practices indicator values above the mean were coded 1 and those below the mean were coded 0. Missing values in the exported dataset were handled using mode imputation prior to model training. The final analytic dataset then underwent feature selection (RFECV to identify top 15 features, followed by domain-knowledge refinement to an optimal set of 10 features) and model evaluation on training/validation/test splits.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (secondary teachers, Shanghai, China) — Teaching Practices (T3TPRA) binary classification
main_findings.target_variable: High vs low instructional practices (above-mean vs below-mean T3TPRA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (accuracy): RF train 0.8191; GBM train 0.8354; XGBoost train 0.8178. Test accuracy: GBM 0.807, RF 0.809, XGBoost 0.786. Best model selection based on accuracy and stability: GBM chosen; iterative feature set of 10 features achieved test accuracy 0.845 with validation mean 0.845 and test-set stability SD 0.015.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 data for secondary teachers in Shanghai, China, the study leveraged Small group work, Quieten the class for lesson, Classroom disciplinary climate (CDC), Assessment and feedback, and Summarizing lesson content to predict high vs low instructional practices, finding that the Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) achieved the best overall balance of test accuracy and stability (test accuracy around 0.807; best 10-feature configuration reached 0.845). This indicates that instructional-practice quality is most strongly associated with specific classroom management and teaching-strategy behaviors, suggesting teacher development should prioritize small-group work, lesson-quieting routines, and structured lesson summarization while monitoring how assessment/feedback and disciplinary climate relate to practice quality.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher microdata for secondary school teachers in Shanghai, China (3,976 teachers across 198 schools in 16 districts) and operationalizes “Teaching Practices” (T3TPRA) as a binary outcome (above-mean = high instructional practices; below-mean = low). After mode imputation for missing values, the authors apply RFECV-based feature selection and then refine to an optimal set of 10 features using domain knowledge. For prediction, they compare Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and XGBoost, and interpret the GBM model using SHAP. In model comparison, GBM shows the best stability and competitive test accuracy (GBM test accuracy 0.807 vs RF 0.809 and XGBoost 0.786), while the best 10-feature configuration reaches test accuracy 0.845 with validation mean 0.845 and SD 0.015. The study’s SHAP-based interpretation reflects predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the paper does not clearly document whether imputation and feature selection were nested within cross-validation folds.
